summary.title: What would a map of your career look like?
summary.one_liner: Career maps can show messy, non-linear paths, and for independent workers the "career possibility space" matters more than a fixed ladder.
takeaways: Careers are easier to map in hindsight, and independent workers lack the conventional career path that salaried roles provide.
Several people have visualized their careers as messy maps, including paths not taken, using tools like Miro templates and mind maps.
Venkatesh Rao's leverage curves idea explains why free agents can stall when they fail to imagine progression.
Career growth in a permissionless world tends to be modular and iterative, favoring experiments and networks over waiting for permission.
Navigate a career by internal strengths rather than external frames; if something feels ridiculously hard, it may be the wrong fit.
summary.summary: Tom Critchlow collects several examples of people visualizing their careers, including Elena Verna's Miro-based career journey, Michael Sklar's map with paths not taken, and an artist's mind map of his work from 1964 to 2014. He draws on Will Larson's idea of a forty-year career and Venkatesh Rao's leverage curves from The Art of Gig to discuss how free agents lack a standard career path. The post then argues for experiments, new networks and modular growth in a permissionless world, and for navigating by internal rather than external reference points. It ends with two reflective questions for the reader about visualizing their own career.
